subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Minimize \(z = 4x + 5y\) subject to \(2x + y \geq 7\), \(2x + 3y \leq 15\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\). Solve using graphical method.
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints are \(2x + y \geq 7\), \(2x + 3y \leq 15\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(2x + y = 7\) meets the axes at \((3.5, 0)\) and \((0, 7)\); \(2x + 3y = 15\) meets them at \((7.5, 0)\) and \((0, 5)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\), \(2x + y = 0 \geq 7\) is false, so the region for \(2x + y \geq 7\) is the side away from the origin; \(2x + 3y = 0 \leq 15\) is true, so the region for \(2x + 3y \leq 15\) is the origin side. Both boundaries are included.

The region does not reach the Y-axis: putting \(x = 0\), the first inequation needs \(y \geq 7\) while the second needs \(y \leq 5\), which is impossible. So the feasible region is a bounded triangle with these vertices:

\((3.5, 0)\): \(2x + y = 7\) meets the X-axis \(y = 0\) (it satisfies \(2x + 3y = 7 \leq 15\)).
\((7.5, 0)\): \(2x + 3y = 15\) meets the X-axis \(y = 0\) (it satisfies \(2x + y = 15 \geq 7\)).
\((1.5, 4)\): \(2x + y = 7\) meets \(2x + 3y = 15\) — subtracting, \(2y = 8\), so \(y = 4\) and \(2x = 7 - 4 = 3\), giving \(x = 1.5\).

| Corner point | \(z = 4x + 5y\) |
|---|---|
| \((3.5, 0)\) | \(14\) |
| \((7.5, 0)\) | \(30\) |
| \((1.5, 4)\) | \(26\) |

The region is bounded, so \(z\) attains its minimum at a corner. The minimum value of \(z\) is \(14\), attained at \((x, y) = (3.5, 0)\).

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Solve the following L.P.P. by graphical method: Maximize \(Z = 6x + 4y\) Subject to \(x \leq 2\), \(x + y \leq 3\), \(- 2x + y \leq 1\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints are \(x \leq 2\), \(x + y \leq 3\), \(-2x + y \leq 1\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(x = 2\) (a vertical line); \(x + y = 3\) meets the axes at \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\); \(-2x + y = 1\) meets them at \((-0.5, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\) we get \(0 \leq 2\), \(0 \leq 3\) and \(0 \leq 1\), all true, so each of the three regions is the origin side of its line, boundaries included. With \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\) the feasible region is a bounded pentagon.

Corner points:

\(O(0, 0)\): the two axes meet.
\((2, 0)\): \(x = 2\) meets the X-axis (it satisfies \(x + y = 2 \leq 3\) and \(-2x + y = -4 \leq 1\)).
\((2, 1)\): \(x = 2\) meets \(x + y = 3\) (it satisfies \(-2x + y = -3 \leq 1\)).
\(\left(\frac{2}{3}, \frac{7}{3}\right)\): \(x + y = 3\) meets \(-2x + y = 1\) — subtracting, \(3x = 2\), so \(x = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(y = 3 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{7}{3}\).
\((0, 1)\): \(-2x + y = 1\) meets the Y-axis.

| Corner point | \(Z = 6x + 4y\) |
|---|---|
| \(O(0,0)\) | \(0\) |
| \((2, 0)\) | \(12\) |
| \((2, 1)\) | \(16\) |
| \(\left(\frac{2}{3}, \frac{7}{3}\right)\) | \(\frac{40}{3} \approx 13.33\) |
| \((0, 1)\) | \(4\) |

The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(16\), attained at \((x, y) = (2, 1)\).

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Minimize \(Z = 7x + y\) subject to \(5x + y \geq 5\), \(x + y \geq 3\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints are \(5x + y \geq 5\), \(x + y \geq 3\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(5x + y = 5\) meets the axes at \((1, 0)\) and \((0, 5)\); \(x + y = 3\) meets them at \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\), \(0 \geq 5\) and \(0 \geq 3\) are both false, so each region is the side away from the origin (boundaries included). The feasible region lies above both lines in the first quadrant and is unbounded above.

Corner points:

\((0, 5)\): \(5x + y = 5\) meets the Y-axis (it satisfies \(x + y = 5 \geq 3\)).
\((0.5, 2.5)\): \(5x + y = 5\) meets \(x + y = 3\) — subtracting, \(4x = 2\), so \(x = 0.5\) and \(y = 2.5\).
\((3, 0)\): \(x + y = 3\) meets the X-axis (it satisfies \(5x + y = 15 \geq 5\)).

| Corner point | \(Z = 7x + y\) |
|---|---|
| \((0, 5)\) | \(5\) |
| \((0.5, 2.5)\) | \(6\) |
| \((3, 0)\) | \(21\) |

The region is unbounded, but since we are minimizing and \(Z \geq 0\) throughout the first quadrant, the minimum is attained at a corner. The minimum value of \(Z\) is \(5\), attained at \((x, y) = (0, 5)\).

solution:

The constraints are \(x + 4y \leq 24\), \(x + y \leq 9\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(x + 4y = 24\) meets the axes at \((24, 0)\) and \((0, 6)\); \(x + y = 9\) meets them at \((9, 0)\) and \((0, 9)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\), \(0 \leq 24\) and \(0 \leq 9\) are both true, so each region is the origin side (boundaries included). The feasible region is a bounded quadrilateral.

Corner points:

\(O(0, 0)\).
\((9, 0)\): \(x + y = 9\) meets the X-axis (it satisfies \(x + 4y = 9 \leq 24\), so it is the binding point on that axis).
\((4, 5)\): \(x + y = 9\) meets \(x + 4y = 24\) — subtracting, \(3y = 15\), so \(y = 5\) and \(x = 4\).

| Corner point | \(Z = 3x + 5y\) |
|---|---|
| \(O(0,0)\) | \(0\) |
| \((9, 0)\) | \(27\) |
| \((4, 5)\) | \(37\) |

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Solve the following linear programming problem: Maximize \(Z = 150x + 250y\) Subject to: \(4x + y \leq 40\), \(3x + 2y \leq 60\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints are \(4x + y \leq 40\), \(3x + 2y \leq 60\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(4x + y = 40\) meets the axes at \((10, 0)\) and \((0, 40)\); \(3x + 2y = 60\) meets them at \((20, 0)\) and \((0, 30)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\), \(0 \leq 40\) and \(0 \leq 60\) are both true, so each region is the origin side (boundaries included). The feasible region is a bounded quadrilateral.

Corner points:

\(O(0, 0)\).
\((10, 0)\): \(4x + y = 40\) meets the X-axis (it satisfies \(3x + 2y = 30 \leq 60\), so it is the binding point on that axis).
\((4, 24)\): \(4x + y = 40\) meets \(3x + 2y = 60\) — from the first, \(y = 40 - 4x\); substituting, \(3x + 80 - 8x = 60\), so \(-5x = -20\), \(x = 4\) and \(y = 24\).
\((0, 30)\): \(3x + 2y = 60\) meets the Y-axis (it satisfies \(4x + y = 30 \leq 40\), so it is the binding point on that axis).

| Corner point | \(Z = 150x + 250y\) |
|---|---|
| \(O(0,0)\) | \(0\) |
| \((10, 0)\) | \(1500\) |
| \((4, 24)\) | \(6600\) |
| \((0, 30)\) | \(7500\) |

The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(7500\), attained at \((x, y) = (0, 30)\).

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Solve the L.P.P. by graphical method. Minimize \(z = 8x + 10y\) subject to \(2x + y \geq 7\), \(2x + 3y \geq 15\), \(y \geq 0\), \(x \geq 0\).
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints are \(2x + y \geq 7\), \(2x + 3y \geq 15\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(2x + y = 7\) meets the axes at \((3.5, 0)\) and \((0, 7)\); \(2x + 3y = 15\) meets them at \((7.5, 0)\) and \((0, 5)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\), \(0 \geq 7\) and \(0 \geq 15\) are both false, so each region is the side away from the origin (boundaries included). The feasible region lies above both lines in the first quadrant and is unbounded above.

Corner points:

\((0, 7)\): \(2x + y = 7\) meets the Y-axis (it satisfies \(2x + 3y = 21 \geq 15\), so it is the binding point on that axis).
\((1.5, 4)\): \(2x + y = 7\) meets \(2x + 3y = 15\) — subtracting, \(2y = 8\), so \(y = 4\) and \(2x = 3\), \(x = 1.5\).
\((7.5, 0)\): \(2x + 3y = 15\) meets the X-axis (it satisfies \(2x + y = 15 \geq 7\), so it is the binding point on that axis).

| Corner point | \(z = 8x + 10y\) |
|---|---|
| \((0, 7)\) | \(70\) |
| \((1.5, 4)\) | \(52\) |
| \((7.5, 0)\) | \(60\) |

The region is unbounded, but since we are minimizing and \(z \geq 0\) throughout the first quadrant, the minimum is attained at a corner. The minimum value of \(z\) is \(52\), attained at \((x, y) = (1.5, 4)\).

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Solve the following L.P.P. by graphical method: Maximize \(z = 10x + 25y\) Subject to: \(0 \leq x \leq 3\), \(0 \leq y \leq 3\), \(x + y \leq 5\). Also find the maximum value of \(z\).
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints \(0 \leq x \leq 3\), \(0 \leq y \leq 3\), \(x + y \leq 5\) mean \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\), \(x \leq 3\), \(y \leq 3\) and \(x + y \leq 5\).

Boundary lines: \(x = 3\) and \(y = 3\) (which together with the axes bound the square \([0,3] \times [0,3]\)), and \(x + y = 5\), meeting the axes at \((5, 0)\) and \((0, 5)\).

Origin test on the slant line: at \((0,0)\), \(0 \leq 5\) is true, so \(x + y \leq 5\) is the origin side. It cuts a corner off the square. The feasible region is a bounded pentagon.

Corner points:

\(O(0, 0)\), \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\): the square's corners on the axes.
\((3, 2)\): \(x = 3\) meets \(x + y = 5\), giving \(y = 2\) (and \(y = 2 \leq 3\)).
\((2, 3)\): \(y = 3\) meets \(x + y = 5\), giving \(x = 2\) (and \(x = 2 \leq 3\)).

| Corner point | \(z = 10x + 25y\) |
|---|---|
| \(O(0,0)\) | \(0\) |
| \((3, 0)\) | \(30\) |
| \((3, 2)\) | \(80\) |
| \((2, 3)\) | \(95\) |
| \((0, 3)\) | \(75\) |

The maximum value of \(z\) is \(95\), attained at \((x, y) = (2, 3)\).

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: Solve the linear programming problem graphically. Maximize: \(z = 3x + 5y\) Subject to: \(x + 4y \leq 24\), \(3x + y \leq 21\), \(x + y \leq 9\), \(x \geq 0,y \geq 0\). Also find the maximum value of \(z\).
solution:
The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below is the complete solution and names every vertex the sketch must show.

The constraints are \(x + 4y \leq 24\), \(3x + y \leq 21\), \(x + y \leq 9\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

Boundary lines: \(x + 4y = 24\) meets the axes at \((24, 0)\) and \((0, 6)\); \(3x + y = 21\) at \((7, 0)\) and \((0, 21)\); \(x + y = 9\) at \((9, 0)\) and \((0, 9)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\) all three inequations hold, so each region is the origin side (boundaries included). The feasible region is a bounded pentagon.

Corner points:

\(O(0, 0)\).
\((7, 0)\): \(3x + y = 21\) meets the X-axis; it is the binding point there, since it gives the smallest of the three x-intercepts.
\((6, 3)\): \(3x + y = 21\) meets \(x + y = 9\) — subtracting, \(2x = 12\), so \(x = 6\) and \(y = 3\) (it satisfies \(x + 4y = 18 \leq 24\)).
\((4, 5)\): \(x + y = 9\) meets \(x + 4y = 24\) — subtracting, \(3y = 15\), so \(y = 5\) and \(x = 4\) (it satisfies \(3x + y = 17 \leq 21\)).
\((0, 6)\): \(x + 4y = 24\) meets the Y-axis; it is the binding point there, since it gives the smallest of the three y-intercepts.

| Corner point | \(z = 3x + 5y\) |
|---|---|
| \(O(0,0)\) | \(0\) |
| \((7, 0)\) | \(21\) |
| \((6, 3)\) | \(33\) |
| \((4, 5)\) | \(37\) |
| \((0, 6)\) | \(30\) |

The maximum value of \(z\) is \(37\), attained at \((x, y) = (4, 5)\).

subtopic: Graphical Solution of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: If the corner points of the feasible solution are \((0,10)\), \((2,2)\) and \((4,0)\) then the point of minimum \(z = 3x + 2y\) is _______.
solution:
**(A)** The optimal value of a linear objective function over a feasible region is attained at a corner point, so evaluate \(z = 3x + 2y\) at each of the three given corner points.

| Corner point | \(z = 3x + 2y\) |
|---|---|
| \((0, 10)\) | \(3(0) + 2(10) = 20\) |
| \((2, 2)\) | \(3(2) + 2(2) = 10\) |
| \((4, 0)\) | \(3(4) + 2(0) = 12\) |

The smallest of \(20\), \(10\), \(12\) is \(10\), so \(z\) is minimum at \((2, 2)\). (Option (D) \((3, 4)\) is not a corner point of the given region at all, so it cannot be tested.)

stem: Solve the following inequations graphically and write the corner points of the feasible region: \(2x + 3y \leq 6,x + y \geq 2,x \geq 0,y \geq 0\)
solution:
The common region should be drawn on graph paper; the work below identifies each half-plane and every corner point the sketch must show.

The inequations are \(2x + 3y \leq 6\), \(x + y \geq 2\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\). Since \(x \geq 0\) and \(y \geq 0\), the region lies in the first quadrant only.

Line \(2x + 3y = 6\): intercepts \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\). At \((0,0)\): \(0 \leq 6\) is true, so the region for \(2x + 3y \leq 6\) is the origin side (boundary included).

Line \(x + y = 2\): intercepts \((2, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\). At \((0,0)\): \(0 \geq 2\) is false, so the region for \(x + y \geq 2\) is the side away from the origin (boundary included).

The two lines meet where \(x + y = 2\) and \(2x + 3y = 6\): substituting \(x = 2 - y\) gives \(4 - 2y + 3y = 6\), so \(y = 2\) and \(x = 0\), i.e. at \((0, 2)\) — both lines cut the Y-axis at the same point.

The feasible region is therefore a bounded triangle, and its corner points are

\((2, 0)\): \(x + y = 2\) meets the X-axis.
\((3, 0)\): \(2x + 3y = 6\) meets the X-axis.
\((0, 2)\): the two lines meet on the Y-axis.

Corner points of the feasible region: \((2, 0)\), \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\).

subtopic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem
stem: A diet of a sick person must contain at least 48 units of vitamin A and 64 units of vitamin B. Two foods \(F_{1}\) and \(F_{2}\) are available. Food \(F_{1}\) costs 6 per unit and food \(F_{2}\) costs 10 per unit. One unit of food \(F_{1}\) contains 6 units of vitamin A and 7 units of vitamin B. One unit of food \(F_{2}\) contains 8 units of vitamin A and 12 units of vitamin B. Find the minimum cost for the diet that consists of mixture of these two foods and also meeting the minimal nutritional requirements.
solution:
**Formulation.** Let \(x\) = number of units of food \(F_{1}\) and \(y\) = number of units of food \(F_{2}\) in the diet. Then \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

| Content | \(F_{1}\) per unit | \(F_{2}\) per unit | Minimum requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vitamin A | 6 | 8 | 48 |
| Vitamin B | 7 | 12 | 64 |
| Cost (Rs.) | 6 | 10 | — |

The cost is \(C = 6x + 10y\), to be minimized. The vitamin requirements give \(6x + 8y \geq 48\), i.e. \(3x + 4y \geq 24\), and \(7x + 12y \geq 64\).

The L.P.P. is: Minimize \(C = 6x + 10y\) subject to \(3x + 4y \geq 24\), \(7x + 12y \geq 64\), \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\).

**Solution.** The feasible region should be drawn on graph paper; the corner-point work below names every vertex the sketch must show.

Boundary lines: \(3x + 4y = 24\) meets the axes at \((8, 0)\) and \((0, 6)\); \(7x + 12y = 64\) meets them at \(\left(\frac{64}{7}, 0\right)\) and \(\left(0, \frac{16}{3}\right)\).

Origin test: at \((0,0)\), \(0 \geq 24\) and \(0 \geq 64\) are both false, so each region is the side away from the origin (boundaries included). The feasible region is unbounded above.

Corner points:

\((0, 6)\): \(3x + 4y = 24\) meets the Y-axis (it satisfies \(7x + 12y = 72 \geq 64\), so it is the binding point on that axis).
\((4, 3)\): \(3x + 4y = 24\) meets \(7x + 12y = 64\) — multiplying the first by 3 gives \(9x + 12y = 72\); subtracting, \(2x = 8\), so \(x = 4\), and then \(12 + 4y = 24\) gives \(y = 3\).
\(\left(\frac{64}{7}, 0\right)\): \(7x + 12y = 64\) meets the X-axis (it satisfies \(3x + 4y = \frac{192}{7} \approx 27.4 \geq 24\), so it is the binding point on that axis).

| Corner point | \(C = 6x + 10y\) |
|---|---|
| \((0, 6)\) | \(60\) |
| \((4, 3)\) | \(54\) |
| \(\left(\frac{64}{7}, 0\right)\) | \(\frac{384}{7} \approx 54.86\) |

The region is unbounded, but since we are minimizing and \(C \geq 0\) throughout the first quadrant, the minimum is attained at a corner. The minimum cost is Rs. \(54\), attained at \(x = 4\) units of \(F_{1}\) and \(y = 3\) units of \(F_{2}\).

Check: vitamin A \(= 6(4) + 8(3) = 48\) units and vitamin B \(= 7(4) + 12(3) = 64\) units, so both requirements are met exactly.
